Oh yes, I would be cautious here. You can make other arguments, such as:

  • Myopia is not entirely genetic, but is also influenced by environmental factors, and sometimes increases dramatically in a population over a short period of time when associated with certain kinds of industrial work.

  • The genes that cause myopia may be different for different ethnic groups. (Although I think myopia should have a high enough fitness cost to make this unlikely - you wouldn't think that genes associated with poor vision would emerge and remain in all human populations independently without being bred out.)

  • The genes associated with high intelligence may differ between ethnic groups. (More likely because intelligence is bound to be so polygenic.)

Still, it is very telling that myopia is yet one more trait that follows the Asian > white > black hierarchy that you see in so many other places. I think of it as hundreds of puzzle pieces: by itself, the prevalence of myopia tells us nothing, but in the context of that racial ranking emerging everywhere else, it's probably meaningful.
